citations.quote: Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Let $(E,\mathcal S,\mu)$ and $(T,\mathcal T,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure spaces. Let a joint probability $\lambda$ on $E\times T$ have nonnegative product-measurable density $p:E\times T\to[0,\infty]$ relative to $\mu\times\nu$. A fixed probability $\rho$ on $(E,\mathcal S)$ is supplied. Put
$$m(y)=\int_E p(x,y)\,\mu(dx),\qquad D=\{y:0<m(y)<\infty\},$$
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_Ap(x,y)\,\mu(dx)}{m(y)},&y\in D,\\ \rho(A),&y\notin D.\end{cases}$$

Then K is an everywhere probability kernel from T to E. If $\beta$ is the second marginal of $\lambda$, then $\beta(D)=1$ and
$$\lambda(A\times B)=\int_B K(y,A)\,\beta(dy).$$

For any random elements X,Y with joint law $\lambda$, $K(Y,\cdot)$ is a regular conditional distribution of X given $\sigma(Y)$. These event identities require no AC. If interpreted with the library's conditional-expectation class existence convention, assume AC. Neither zero nor infinite marginal-density fibres are normalized by the displayed quotient.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let
$m,n \ge 1$. Under the identification
$$\mathbb R^{m+n}=\mathbb R^m \times \mathbb R^n,$$
the product measure $\lambda_m \times \lambda_n$ and the Euclidean Lebesgue
measure $\lambda_{m+n}$ agree on every Borel subset of $\mathbb R^{m+n}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume AC. Then countable choice holds. Moreover, if $R\subseteq X\times X$ is serial on a nonempty set X and $a\in X$, there is a sequence $(x_n)_{n\ge0}$ with $x_0=a$ and $x_n R x_{n+1}$ for every n. Thus the countable and dependent choices required by the probability-product suppliers are available under AC.

Assume AC. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph, with $E$ a set of unordered two-element subsets of $V$. A clique is a nonempty subset $C\subseteq V$ whose distinct vertices are adjacent. Let $(X_i)_{i\in V}$ be random elements on a common probability space, and for $U\subseteq V$ put $\mathcal F_U=\sigma(X_i:i\in U)$, with $\mathcal F_\emptyset=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$. A path is a finite sequence of distinct vertices with adjacent consecutive vertices; $C$ separates $A$ from $B$ if every path from $A$ to $B$ meets $C$. The pairwise Markov property is $\mathcal F_{\{i\}}\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F_{\{j\}}\mid\mathcal F_{V\setminus\{i,j\}}$ whenever $i\ne j$ and $\{i,j\}\notin E$. The global Markov property is $\mathcal F_A\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F_B\mid\mathcal F_C$ whenever $A,B,C\subseteq V$ are pairwise disjoint and $C$ separates $A$ from $B$. If each $X_i$ takes values in a finite nonempty state space $\mathcal X_i$, a finite-state clique-factorized mass function on $G$ is $p(x)=Z^{-1}\prod_{C\in\mathcal C}\psi_C(x_C)$, where $\mathcal C$ is a finite collection of nonempty cliques, $\psi_C:\prod_{i\in C}\mathcal X_i\to(0,\infty)$, and $Z=\sum_{x\in\prod_{i\in V}\mathcal X_i}\prod_{C\in\mathcal C}\psi_C(x_C)$. The product state space and sum are finite, and every potential is positive and finite, so $0<Z<\infty$ and $p$ is a probability mass function. No equivalence between the clique-factorized class and either Markov property is asserted here.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Fix distinct $i,j$. By [A1], [F1] and [F2], the joint density of $X$ is the stated nondegenerate Gaussian density; here positive definiteness is an additional hypothesis beyond the singular-covariance multivariate-normal definition.

Reorder coordinates so $Y=(X_i,X_j)$ and $Z=(X_k)_{k\notin\{i,j\}}$. In the correspondingly permuted precision matrix write $\Theta=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\B^T&C\end{pmatrix}$, where $A=\begin{pmatrix}a&c\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$. For every nonzero $u\in\mathbb R^2$, $u^TAu=(u,0)^T\Theta(u,0)>0$, so $A$ is positive definite and $\det A=ad-c^2>0$. If $p=2$, the $Z$ coordinate is a singleton and the following conditional-density calculation is the unconditional bivariate density.

For $p>2$, [F7] supplies the countable-choice hypothesis of [F6], so the joint Euclidean density in [F2] is also a density relative to $\lambda_2\otimes\lambda_{p-2}$. Put $u=y-\mu_Y$, $w=z-\mu_Z$, and $D=C-B^TA^{-1}B$. For nonzero $w$, $(-A^{-1}Bw,w)^T\Theta(-A^{-1}Bw,w)=w^TDw>0$, hence $D$ is positive definite. Completing the square gives $u^TAu+2u^TBw+w^TCw=(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw)+w^TDw$. The section integral over $y$ is therefore positive and finite for every $z$: its $y$ factor is the normalized two-dimensional Gaussian density with precision $A$, multiplied by a finite positive constant.

For $p>2$, use the explicit filler probability concentrated at $(0,0)$ on $\mathbb R^2$ in [F3]; the positive finite marginal sections from step 3.1 show that the conditional law at every $z$ has density $\frac{\sqrt{\det A}}{2\pi}\exp(-\tfrac12(u+A^{-1}Bw)^TA(u+A^{-1}Bw))$. It is the bivariate normal law with mean $\mu_Y-A^{-1}B(z-\mu_Z)$ and covariance $A^{-1}$. For $p=2$, this is the unconditional law with covariance $\Theta^{-1}=A^{-1}$.

If $\Theta_{ij}=c=0$, then $A$ is diagonal and the conditional density in step 4.1 is a product of two univariate Gaussian densities for every $z$. Its conditional expectations therefore factor for all bounded measurable coordinate functions; [F4] gives $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$.

Conversely, suppose $X_i\perp\!\!\!\perp X_j\mid\sigma(Z)$. Apply [F4] to the four bounded pairs formed from $\cos(X_i),\sin(X_i)$ and $\cos(X_j),\sin(X_j)$ and combine the resulting identities. For almost every $z$, the conditional joint characteristic function at $(1,1)$ equals the product of its conditional marginal characteristic functions. By [F1], [F4] and [F5], the joint characteristic function from step 4.1 is $\exp(i(m_1(z)+m_2(z))-\tfrac12((A^{-1})_{11}+2(A^{-1})_{12}+(A^{-1})_{22}))$, whereas that product omits the middle covariance term. Equality implies $\exp(-(A^{-1})_{12})=1$, and since $(A^{-1})_{12}$ is real this forces $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$.

The inverse of $A$ is $(ad-c^2)^{-1}\begin{pmatrix}d&-c\\-c&a\end{pmatrix}$. Since $\det A>0$, $(A^{-1})_{12}=0$ if and only if $c=0$, which is exactly $\Theta_{ij}=0$. Steps 5.1 and 5.2 prove the two implications; by [F8], these are exactly the nonedge and conditional-independence cases of the Gaussian pairwise Markov graph.

Steps 5.2 and 6.1 prove conditional independence implies Θij=0.

citations.quote: For $N,p\ge1$ and data $x_1,\ldots,x_N\in\mathbb R^p$, put $\bar x=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N x_r$ and $S=N^{-1}\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\bar x)(x_r-\bar x)^T$. For any symmetric positive-semidefinite $S$ and any $\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$, set $\ell_S(\Theta)=\log\det\Theta-\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)$, where $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is the cone of symmetric positive-definite $p\times p$ matrices. Define $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^p\sum_{j=1}^p|\Theta_{ij}|$, including diagonal entries, and for $\lambda>0$ define $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\|\Theta\|_1$. The off-diagonal-only convention $F^{\mathrm{off}}_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)=\ell_S(\Theta)-\lambda\sum_{i\ne j}|\Theta_{ij}|$ is a separate objective.

Assume AC. Let $d\ge1$, $m\in\mathbb R^d$, and let $\Sigma$ be a real symmetric positive-definite $d\times d$ matrix. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then its law has Lebesgue density
$$f_{m,\Sigma}(x)=(2\pi)^{-d/2}\det(\Sigma)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\tfrac12(x-m)^T\Sigma^{-1}(x-m)\right), \qquad x\in\mathbb R^d.$$

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $n\ge1$ and let $(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. For each $j<n$, let
$K_j$ be a probability kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T_j,\Tau_j)$, let
$\nu_j$ be sigma-finite on $(T_j,\Tau_j)$, and let
$f_j:S\times T_j\to[0,\infty]$ be a specified
jointly measurable function such that
$$K_j(s,B)=\int_B f_j(s,t_j)\,\nu_j(dt_j)\qquad(B\in\Tau_j).$$
On the finite product spaces, let $K=\bigotimes_{j<n}K_j$ be the product
probability kernel, let $\nu=\bigotimes_{j<n}\nu_j$, and put
$$f(s,t)=\prod_{j<n}f_j(s,t_j),$$
using the extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=0$. Then $f$ is jointly
measurable and, for every $s\in S$, it is a density of $K(s,\cdot)$
with respect to $\nu$ on the entire product sigma-algebra.

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

derivations.claim: Each independent observation with the common law in [F3] has the density in [F2]. On the one-point source $\{*\}$, the constant law $K_r(*,\cdot)=N_p(\mu,\Sigma)$ is a probability kernel: its sections are probability measures and each evaluation map is constant, hence measurable [F4]. The density $f_r(*,x)=f_{\mu,\Theta}(x)$ is continuous in $x$ and constant in $*$, hence jointly measurable; [F5] gives the product law density $\prod_{r=1}^N f_{\mu,\Theta}(x_r)$. By [F6], independence identifies this product law with the joint observation law. Its log-likelihood for fixed $\mu$ and $\Theta$ is $$L(\mu,\Theta)=-\frac{Np}{2}\log(2\pi)+\frac N2\log\det\Theta-\frac12\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\mu)^T\Theta(x_r-\mu).$$

Write $y_r=x_r-\bar x$, so $\sum_r y_r=0$ and $x_r-\mu=y_r+(\bar x-\mu)$. Expanding and summing removes the cross term: $$\sum_{r=1}^N(x_r-\mu)^T\Theta(x_r-\mu)=\sum_{r=1}^Ny_r^T\Theta y_r+N(\mu-\bar x)^T\Theta(\mu-\bar x).$$
Positive definiteness of $\Theta$ makes the last quadratic term nonnegative and equal to zero exactly at $\mu=\bar x$. Therefore $\bar x$ uniquely maximizes $L(\mu,\Theta)$ over $\mu$.

By [F1], $\sum_r y_ry_r^T=NS$. Cyclicity of the finite matrix trace gives $\sum_r y_r^T\Theta y_r=\sum_r\operatorname{tr}(\Theta y_ry_r^T)=N\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)$. Substituting this identity and $\mu=\bar x$ into step 1.1 yields the displayed profile log-likelihood and its normalization.

Statement requires Σ≻0 but permits singular sample covariance S; the proof never inverts S.
Step 3.1 shows the unique profile point μ=x̄; the proof forms no quotient at an endpoint.
Step 1.1 uses the density supplier under its explicit AC hypothesis; the finite product has N≥1 factors.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$
  now a finite real or complex number.

For an integrable real random variable,
$$\mathbb E[X]=\mathbb E[X^+]-\mathbb E[X^-],$$
where $X^+$ and $X^-$ are its positive and negative parts.

derivations.claim: The state space $\{0,1\}^m\times\{0,1\}^n$ has $2^{m+n}$ elements. Every term $\exp(-E(v,h))$ is finite and positive, so their finite sum $Z$ is finite and positive; therefore $p$ is a probability mass function.

For fixed $v$, put $c_j=b_j+(W^Tv)_j$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j\exp(h_jc_j)$, and summing over binary $h$ gives $\exp(a^Tv)\prod_j(1+\exp(c_j))$. Thus $p(h\mid v)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(c_j)/(1+\exp(c_j))=\sigma(c_j)$.

For fixed $h$, put $d_i=a_i+(Wh)_i$. Then $\exp(-E(v,h))=\exp(b^Th)\prod_i\exp(v_id_i)$, and summing over binary $v$ gives $\exp(b^Th)\prod_i(1+\exp(d_i))$. Hence $p(v\mid h)$ is the product of Bernoulli masses with success probabilities $\exp(d_i)/(1+\exp(d_i))=\sigma(d_i)$.

For fixed observed $v$, $p(v)=Z^{-1}\exp(a^Tv)\sum_h\exp(b^Th+v^TWh)$. Differentiating these finite sums gives $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log p(v)=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z$; the same calculation gives $\partial_{a_i}\log p(v)=v_i-\partial_{a_i}\log Z$ and $\partial_{b_j}\log p(v)=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\partial_{b_j}\log Z$.

The product conditional mass functions in steps 2.1–2.2 make the conditional expectations of any bounded measurable functions of disjoint coordinates factor into the product of their conditional expectations. By [F1]–[F2], each layer is therefore conditionally independent given the other in the stated sigma-algebra sense. This use of the conditional-expectation convention is the only proof point needing [A1].

Differentiating the finite partition sum yields $\partial_{W_{ij}}\log Z=\sum_{v',h'}v_i'h_j'p(v',h')=\mathbb E_p[V_iH_j]$, $\partial_{a_i}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[V_i]$, and $\partial_{b_j}\log Z=\mathbb E_p[H_j]$. Substitution in step 2.3 gives the exact gradients in the Definition.

For each visible state $v$, $\sum_{v'}K(v,v')=\sum_h p(h\mid v)\sum_{v'}p(v'\mid h)=\sum_hp(h\mid v)=1$. Thus K is a stochastic matrix and each $q_k^v$ is a well-defined finite probability distribution. A $C^2$ function on an open convex set is convex if and only if its Hessian is positive semidefinite at every point. Hessians and their quadratic forms have the conventions of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]], [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]].

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.

derivations.claim: By the all-entry objective definition [F1] and the nonnegative-operator factorization [F2], write $S=R^TR$. Thus $\operatorname{tr}(S\Theta)=\operatorname{tr}(R\Theta R^T)\ge0$ for $\Theta\succ0$. Also $\|\Theta\|_1=\sum_{i,j}|\Theta_{ij}|\ge\sum_i\Theta_{ii}=\operatorname{tr}\Theta$, since positive-definite matrices have positive diagonal entries.

The cone $\mathbb S_{++}^p$ is open and convex: positive quadratic forms remain positive under sufficiently small symmetric perturbations, and convex combinations of positive quadratic forms remain positive. For symmetric $H$, determinant expansion gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}\log\det(\Theta+tH)\right|_{t=0}=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H)$. Differentiating $(\Theta+tH)(\Theta+tH)^{-1}=I$ gives $\left.\frac{d}{dt}(\Theta+tH)^{-1}\right|_{t=0}=-\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}$, so the second directional derivative is $-\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)$.

By [F3], the eigenvalues $t_1,\ldots,t_p$ of $\Theta\succ0$ are positive and $\log\det\Theta=\sum_k\log t_k$, $\operatorname{tr}\Theta=\sum_k t_k$. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\sum_{k=1}^p h(t_k)$ for $h(t)=\log t-\lambda t$. The function $h$ is bounded above and tends to $-\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$ or $t\to\infty$. For any $c$, the upper level set $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\ge c$ therefore forces each eigenvalue into a compact interval $[a_c,b_c]\subset(0,\infty)$: if $M=\sup_{t>0}h(t)$, then each $h(t_k)\ge c-(p-1)M$. These matrices form a closed bounded set of symmetric matrices contained in $\mathbb S_{++}^p$, hence a compact set. Taking $c=F_{S,\lambda}(I)$ gives a nonempty compact upper level set, and continuity of $F$ yields a maximizer.

Let $B=\Theta^{-1/2}H\Theta^{-1/2}$, using the positive square root from the orthonormal eigenbasis [F3]. Then $B$ is symmetric and $\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}H\Theta^{-1}H)=\operatorname{tr}(B^2)=\|B\|_F^2$, strictly positive when $H\ne0$. Thus the second derivative of $\log\det$ along every nonconstant segment is strictly negative, giving its strict chord inequality. The Hessian of $-\log\det$ is positive semidefinite by step 1.2, so [F4] gives convexity in the chord sense of [F5]. The trace term is linear and the entrywise $\ell^1$ norm is convex by the triangle inequality, so its negative is concave; adding these terms preserves the strict chord inequality. Hence $F_{S,\lambda}$ is strictly concave on its open convex domain.

Put $G=\Theta^{-1}-S$. At a maximizer every feasible one-coordinate directional derivative is at most zero, and when the objective is differentiable in both directions its derivative is zero. Since $\Theta_{ii}>0$, the diagonal penalty is locally differentiable with slope $1$, so the diagonal equation is $G_{ii}-\lambda=0$ and $\Gamma_{ii}=1$. For $i<j$, a symmetric perturbation by $t(E_{ij}+E_{ji})$ has smooth derivative $2G_{ij}t$ and changes the penalty by $2\lambda(|\Theta_{ij}+t|-|\Theta_{ij}|)$. If $\Theta_{ij}\ne0$, testing both signs of small $t$ gives $G_{ij}=\lambda\operatorname{sign}(\Theta_{ij})$. If $\Theta_{ij}=0$, taking $t>0$ gives $G_{ij}\le\lambda$ and taking $t<0$ gives $G_{ij}\ge-\lambda$. Defining $\Gamma_{ij}=\Gamma_{ji}=G_{ij}/\lambda$ at zero and the sign otherwise yields the stated KKT equation for the all-entry penalty [F1].

Conversely, suppose $\Theta\succ0$ and a symmetric $\Gamma$ satisfies the stated entrywise conditions and $\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma=0$. Put $T=\Theta^{-1/2}\Theta'\Theta^{-1/2}$ for any $\Theta'\succ0$; its eigenvalues $t_r$ are positive. Since $\log t\le t-1$ for $t>0$ (the function $t-1-\log t$ has its minimum $0$ at $t=1$), $\log\det\Theta'-\log\det\Theta=\sum_r\log t_r\le\operatorname{tr}(T)-p=\operatorname{tr}(\Theta^{-1}(\Theta'-\Theta))$. For each scalar $x$ and each allowed subgradient $\gamma$ of $|x|$, $|y|\ge|x|+\gamma(y-x)$: if $x\ne0$, this follows from $|y|\ge\operatorname{sign}(x)y$, while for $x=0$ it follows from $|\gamma|\le1$. Summing gives $\|\Theta'\|_1\ge\|\Theta\|_1+\sum_{i,j}\Gamma_{ij}(\Theta'_{ij}-\Theta_{ij})$ for the all-entry objective [F1]. Combining these bounds with the linear trace term and the KKT equation yields $F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta')-F_{S,\lambda}(\Theta)\le\operatorname{tr}((\Theta^{-1}-S-\lambda\Gamma)(\Theta'-\Theta))=0$. Thus every such KKT point is a maximizer. The maximizer exists by step 2.1 and is unique by strict concavity from step 2.2, so the KKT condition is both necessary and sufficient for that unique optimum.

Thus the graph whose edges are exactly the nonzero off-diagonal entries of $\Theta$ is the Gaussian pairwise conditional-dependence graph.

Assume AC. Let $G=(V,E)$ be a finite simple undirected graph, with $E$ a set of unordered two-element subsets of $V$. A clique is a nonempty subset $C\subseteq V$ whose distinct vertices are adjacent. Let $(X_i)_{i\in V}$ be random elements on a common probability space, and for $U\subseteq V$ put $\mathcal F_U=\sigma(X_i:i\in U)$, with $\mathcal F_\emptyset=\{\emptyset,\Omega\}$. A path is a finite sequence of distinct vertices with adjacent consecutive vertices; $C$ separates $A$ from $B$ if every path from $A$ to $B$ meets $C$. The pairwise Markov property is $\mathcal F_{\{i\}}\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F_{\{j\}}\mid\mathcal F_{V\setminus\{i,j\}}$ whenever $i\ne j$ and $\{i,j\}\notin E$. The global Markov property is $\mathcal F_A\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal F_B\mid\mathcal F_C$ whenever $A,B,C\subseteq V$ are pairwise disjoint and $C$ separates $A$ from $B$. If each $X_i$ takes values in a finite nonempty state space $\mathcal X_i$, a finite-state clique-factorized mass function on $G$ is $p(x)=Z^{-1}\prod_{C\in\mathcal C}\psi_C(x_C)$, where $\mathcal C$ is a finite collection of nonempty cliques, $\psi_C:\prod_{i\in C}\mathcal X_i\to(0,\infty)$, and $Z=\sum_{x\in\prod_{i\in V}\mathcal X_i}\prod_{C\in\mathcal C}\psi_C(x_C)$. The product state space and sum are finite, and every potential is positive and finite, so $0<Z<\infty$ and $p$ is a probability mass function. No equivalence between the clique-factorized class and either Markov property is asserted here.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Let $m,n\ge1$, visible states $v\in\{0,1\}^m$, hidden states $h\in\{0,1\}^n$, biases $a\in\mathbb R^m$ and $b\in\mathbb R^n$, and weights $W\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}$; a finite bipartite graph is specified by requiring $W_{ij}=0$ at every absent visible-hidden edge. Define $E(v,h)=-a^Tv-b^Th-v^TWh$, $Z=\sum_{v,h}\exp(-E(v,h))$, and $p(v,h)=Z^{-1}\exp(-E(v,h))$; $Z$ is finite and positive. Set $p(v)=\sum_h p(v,h)$, and let $V,H$ be the coordinate variables under $p$. For a finite mass function $q$, write $\mathbb E_q[g]=\sum_xq(x)g(x)$. With $\sigma(t)=(1+\exp(-t))^{-1}$, and $\operatorname{Bernoulli}(u;r)$ the mass on $\{0,1\}$ with probability $r$ at $1$, the layer conditionals factorize as
$$p(h\mid v)=\prod_{j=1}^n\operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(h_j;\sigma\!\left(b_j+(W^Tv)_j\right)\right),\qquad p(v\mid h)=\prod_{i=1}^m\operatorname{Bernoulli}\!\left(v_i;\sigma\!\left(a_i+(Wh)_i\right)\right),$$
so each layer is conditionally independent given the other. For one observed $v$, the exact gradients are
$$\frac{\partial\log p(v)}{\partial W_{ij}}=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\mathbb E_p[V_iH_j],\qquad \frac{\partial\log p(v)}{\partial a_i}=v_i-\mathbb E_p[V_i],\qquad \frac{\partial\log p(v)}{\partial b_j}=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\mathbb E_p[H_j].$$
These are ambient derivatives in all parameters, evaluated at the specified $W$; when a graph fixes absent-edge weights to zero, retain only allowed-edge derivatives as free parameters. Define $K(v,v')=\sum_h p(h\mid v)p(v'\mid h)$, a row-stochastic transition matrix. Starting from $q_0^v=\delta_v$, let $q_k^v=q_0^vK^k$ for a finite integer $k\ge1$. For one observed $v$, define the finite contrastive-divergence components by
$$\widehat g^{(k)}_{W_{ij}}(v)=v_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\sum_{v'}q_k^v(v')v'_i\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v')}[h_j],\quad \widehat g^{(k)}_{a_i}(v)=v_i-\sum_{v'}q_k^v(v')v'_i,\quad \widehat g^{(k)}_{b_j}(v)=\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v)}[h_j]-\sum_{v'}q_k^v(v')\mathbb E_{p(h\mid v')}[h_j].$$
They replace the exact negative-phase expectations under $p(v')$ by expectations under the finite $k$-step law $q_k^v$ and conditional hidden law $p(h\mid v')$. This finite-chain statistic is an approximation; no equality to the exact likelihood gradient or chain-convergence claim is asserted.

Assume the axiom of choice so that the library's conditional-expectation
classes are available. Let $Y$ and $Z$ be random elements and let
$\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ be a sigma-algebra. We say that $Y$ and $Z$ are
**conditionally independent given $\mathcal G$**, and write
$Y\perp\!\!\!\perp Z\mid\mathcal G$, if for every pair of bounded measurable
real functions $f,g$,
$$ \mathbb E[f(Y)g(Z)\mid\mathcal G] =\mathbb E[f(Y)\mid\mathcal G]\, \mathbb E[g(Z)\mid\mathcal G]\quad\text{a.s.} $$
This is an equality of almost-everywhere classes and hence does not depend on
representatives.

For sigma-algebras $\mathcal H_1,\mathcal H_2\subseteq\mathcal F$, the notation
$\mathcal H_1\perp\!\!\!\perp\mathcal H_2\mid\mathcal G$ means the same identity
for every bounded $\mathcal H_1$-measurable $U$ and bounded
$\mathcal H_2$-measurable $V$.

The definition is symmetric. If $\mathcal G=\{\varnothing,\Omega\}$ modulo
null sets, it reduces to ordinary independence. If one side is
$\mathcal G$-measurable, conditional independence is automatic because that
factor is already known when conditioning. The choices of the zero function or
the constant-one function cause no exceptional case.

Input an integer $p\ge2$, a real symmetric positive-semidefinite matrix $S\in\mathbb S_+^p$, a real $\lambda>0$, and positive integers $R,K$. The output is either `failure` or a matrix $\Theta\in\mathbb S_{++}^p$. Let $I_p$ be the $p\times p$ identity, $t_+=\max(t,0)$, $\operatorname{sign}(t)=1$ for $t>0$, $0$ for $t=0$, and $-1$ for $t<0$, and $\mathsf{Soft}(t,\lambda)=\operatorname{sign}(t)(|t|-\lambda)_+$. Initialize $W=S+\lambda I_p$.

For each outer sweep $r=1,\ldots,R$, and within it for each original-coordinate index $j=1,\ldots,p$, use the temporary coordinate order $\pi_j=(1,\ldots,j-1,j+1,\ldots,p,j)$. Form the same reindexing of both matrices, $S^{(j)}_{ab}=S_{\pi_j(a),\pi_j(b)}$ and $W^{(j)}_{ab}=W_{\pi_j(a),\pi_j(b)}$, for $1\le a,b\le p$. Set $V=(W^{(j)}_{ab})_{a,b<p}$, $s=(S^{(j)}_{a,p})_{a<p}$, and $d=W^{(j)}_{pp}$. Initialize $\beta=0\in\mathbb R^{p-1}$. For each of $K$ inner sweeps, update coordinates $\ell=1,\ldots,p-1$ in increasing order: if $V_{\ell\ell}\le0$, return `failure`; otherwise set
$$\beta_\ell\leftarrow\frac{\mathsf{Soft}\!\left(s_\ell-\sum_{\substack{1\le k<p\\k\ne\ell}}V_{\ell k}\beta_k,\lambda\right)}{V_{\ell\ell}}.$$

After the inner sweeps, form $\widetilde W^{(j)}=\begin{pmatrix}V&V\beta\\(V\beta)^T&d\end{pmatrix}$. Restore original indexing by forming the candidate matrix $W^{\mathrm{cand}}$ with $W^{\mathrm{cand}}_{\pi_j(a),\pi_j(b)}=\widetilde W^{(j)}_{ab}$ for all $1\le a,b\le p$. Compute a symmetric eigendecomposition of $W^{\mathrm{cand}}$; if any eigenvalue is nonpositive, return `failure`. Otherwise set $W=W^{\mathrm{cand}}$ before proceeding to the next original-coordinate index $j$. After all $R$ sweeps, return $\Theta=W^{-1}$. This bounded truncation of the coupled block and lasso updates makes no convergence or optimizer claim.

derivations.claim: Initially $W$ is symmetric, and for every nonzero $x\in\mathbb R^p$, $x^TWx=x^TSx+\lambda\|x\|^2\ge\lambda\|x\|^2>0$. Thus initialization is positive definite. If the current $W$ is positive definite, reindexing both its rows and columns only reindexes this quadratic form. For a nonzero $z\in\mathbb R^{p-1}$, extending $z$ by a last zero in the temporary ordering gives $z^TVz>0$. Hence $V$ is positive definite and $V_{\ell\ell}=e_\ell^TVe_\ell>0$ at each coordinate.

Hold all coordinates except $\beta_\ell=t$ fixed, and write $v=V_{\ell\ell}>0$ and $r=s_\ell-\sum_{k\ne\ell}V_{\ell k}\beta_k$. Expanding the symmetric quadratic gives $Q_{V,s}(\beta)=q(t)+C$, where $q(t)=\tfrac12vt^2-rt+\lambda|t|$ and $C$ is independent of $t$. Put $a=(r-\lambda)/v$ if $r>\lambda$, $a=0$ if $|r|\le\lambda$, and $a=(r+\lambda)/v$ if $r<-\lambda$. In these three cases respectively put $u=1$, $u=r/\lambda$, and $u=-1$. Then $va-r+\lambda u=0$, $|u|\le1$, and $ua=|a|$, so $|t|-|a|-u(t-a)=|t|-ut\ge0$. Consequently $q(t)-q(a)=\tfrac12v(t-a)^2+\lambda(|t|-|a|-u(t-a))\ge\tfrac12v(t-a)^2$, and the lower bound is strictly positive whenever $t\ne a$. Thus $a=\mathsf{Soft}(r,\lambda)/v$ is the unique coordinate minimizer. All quantities are real and division is by a positive number, so finitely many such updates produce a finite real vector $\beta$; the nonpositive-diagonal guard cannot fire while the current $W$ is positive definite.

For such a block, $V\beta$ and $d$ are finite and the block candidate $\begin{pmatrix}V&V\beta\\(V\beta)^T&d\end{pmatrix}$ is symmetric. Restoring original indexing preserves symmetry. By [F2] any symmetric candidate $A$ has a representation $A=UDU^T$ with $U$ orthogonal and $D$ real diagonal. The identity $x^TAx=\sum_iD_{ii}(U^Tx)_i^2$ shows that $A$ is positive definite if all $D_{ii}>0$; conversely applying positive definiteness to $x=Ue_i$ shows that every $D_{ii}>0$. Thus the candidate guard accepts exactly the positive-definite candidates. Initialization, the within-block reasoning and this acceptance rule give induction over all reached blocks: every accepted $W$ is symmetric positive definite, and each later block again has the properties proved above until a candidate guard returns `failure`.

There are at most $Rp$ blocks, each with $K(p-1)$ coordinate updates and one finite-dimensional eigenvalue test; early failure only decreases these counts. Every reached operation is well-defined by the preceding steps and the stipulated exact matrix operations, so execution terminates with failure or completes all blocks. In the latter case the final $W=UDU^T$ has positive diagonal eigenvalues by step 3.1. Hence $W^{-1}=UD^{-1}U^T$ exists, is symmetric and has $x^TW^{-1}x=\sum_iD_{ii}^{-1}(U^Tx)_i^2>0$ for every nonzero $x$. This proves every asserted property without a convergence or global-optimizer inference.
